ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are 7 squares in the figure. Mark according to the specified method: the upper left is A, the middle left is B, the middle square with the question mark is C, the middle right is D, the upper right is E, directly below C is F, and the lowest is G. From the figure it can be seen that C touches A, B, D, E, F respectively by an edge or a corner; the only square not adjacent to C is G. Reasoning: If C is filled with k, where k is 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6, then the two numbers consecutive with k, k-1 and k+1, must both be placed in squares not adjacent to C. But there is only one square not adjacent to C, G, and it is impossible to place two different numbers at the same time, so C cannot be 2 to 6. Thus C can only be the endpoint number 1 or 7. Verification of feasibility: If C=1, one can fill G=2, A=3, B=5, D=4, E=6, F=7; among adjacent squares there are no consecutive numbers. Changing this filling by x becoming 8-x to its complement can obtain a feasible filling with C=7. Therefore the numbers that can be filled in the question-mark square are 1 or 7.

method.method_draft: Label the seven fields from the image as: top-left A, middle-left B, question field C, middle-right D, top-right E, field below C as F, and bottom field G. From the image, C touches A, B, D, E, and F by an edge or corner, and its only non-adjacent field is G. From the text, consecutive numbers cannot be placed in adjacent fields. If C contained any number 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6, then both neighboring numbers k-1 and k+1 would have to avoid all five fields adjacent to C, but there is only one non-adjacent field G available, impossible. Therefore C can only be 1 or 7. Then verify both are possible by giving an example filling: for C=1, put G=2 and arrange the remaining fields so no adjacent pair is consecutive, e.g. A=3, B=5, D=4, E=6, F=7. By reversing/complementing the numbers, C=7 is also possible.

method.method_draft: Model the image as a graph whose vertices are the seven fields, with edges between fields sharing an edge or corner. Equivalently, build the complement graph of allowed consecutive placements: two consecutive numbers may occupy two vertices only if the corresponding fields are non-adjacent in the image. In the image, the question-mark field C is adjacent to every field except the bottommost central field G, so in the allowed-consecutive complement graph C has degree 1, connected only to G. The sequence of fields carrying 1, 2, 3, ..., 7 must form a Hamiltonian path in this complement graph, because each consecutive number pair must lie on an allowed non-adjacent pair. A vertex of degree 1 in such a Hamiltonian path can only be an endpoint of the path, so C must carry either 1 or 7. To confirm feasibility, exhibit an allowed path such as C-G-A-D-B-E-F through all fields; assigning numbers 1 through 7 along this path gives C=1, and assigning them in the reverse direction gives C=7.
